questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Good international student environment, opportunity to improve my French.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Really recommend going to Geneva for exchange, because of its very social exchange student environment, there are both ESN (Erasmus Student Network) + UNIGE’s own welcome days and intro week events. Those are really good for making new friends. Also the city is a good size - small enough to get a grip of it but big enough to keep exploring new places. Plus the amount of new exchange students is good - approx. 300-400 people, so that you’ll get to know most of them, (or at least reckognize familiar faces), since you bump into each other at uni or go to the same events in the city.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy, good help from the connected Erasmus Student coordinators at UCPH + UNIGE. The course catalogue wasn’t fully updated before my arrival in Geneva, which made it a bit harder and more stressful putting together a course schedule/study plan + I noticed some of the courses were overlapping.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Welcome days/Introduction week for all exhange students + emails with important information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Look at the course catalogue thoroughly before going, because some courses might be overlapping or have “tutorat”/class teaching at the same time at the same time as other courses.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
It's not directly "on-campus" but it's student accommodation sites around the city - either the big student dorm, La Cité Universitaire de Genève, where I stayed, or shared appartments for students (where you're approx 4 people sharing an appartment - these are kinda big). Signing up for these are both on the website
Logetud.ch

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Not the best cooking facilities at La Cité Universitaire. Small kitchen, one stove, the smallest oven I've seen. But it worked out. There was also a microwave.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I stayed at La Cité Universitaire de Genève, which is a big student dorm, and one of the cheaper options in terms of accommodation. I liked it, a lot of my friends lived there and I met many nice people living there. I would recommend saying yes if offered. It's really trashy though and not like Danish dorms/kollegier. These are kinda worn out. At La Cité Universitaire you get a good sized room with big windows (and usually nice view), live on a hallway with 7 others - and then two hallways (total of 16 pers) share 1 kitchen (can be kinda cramped). The shared appartments at Rue de la Tambourine in the Carouge area are 100 CHF cheaper and also really nice - but a bit further away. I would NOT recommend saying yes to any other accommodation other than La Cité Universitaire de Genève or other student accommodation in Champel, Plainpalais or Carouge. I got offered a student accommodation close to the airport at 23 Chemin des Corbillettes, which I'm really happy, I said no to, because it's super far away and only a few people live there (one of my friends lived there and felt isolated).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you sign up time in advance for student accommodation, you'll definitely get a place via the univeristy to stay - which is the easiest option and most affordable. They are gonna tear down one of the big building blocks, that La Cité Universitaire consists of in autumn 2025 though, so that might make it harder for exchange students to finding a place to stay, but idk.. Otherwise La Ciguë has really good and cheap rooms in shared student appartments (this is a private social initiative)

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have the first weeks of the semester to trying out several different courses and then register later, it’s nice because you can try out some before signing up. I did find creating your own study plan/course plan yourself a bit stressful, and making it work without having (or at least not many) overlapping courses. It can be tricky since L'UNIGE mostly have 3 and 6 ECTS courses, and also it’s your task to do make an actually working study plan, I didn’t receive any help whatsoever.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
Not a lot, you’ll have to find the right courses that adds up to 30 ECTS yourself. I think this is pretty common and pretty much everyone going on exchange has to do this, I just wasen’t quite aware that it’s basically just our own problem, if you can’t make the study plan work out and get accepted on the right courses. I did get enrolled to all the classes I wanted (7 in total, because I took 4 x 3 ECTS courses plus some 6 ECTS courses). I’ve not heard of people not getting in to the courses, they wanted to take - I don’t think this i a problem for anyone at L’UNIGE luckily. 
I did write an e-mail to L’UNIGE about getting permission to take courses from more than 2 faculties (normally you’re only allowed to choose from 2), because I struggled with finding relevant courses only choosing from 2 (and them being mostly in English), but they were super nice and gave me permission, since the course I wanted from the third faculty was relevant for my study area.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I managed to make a nice study plan, with courses from Social Science, Environmental Science, and Economy and Management. The geography department at L'UNIGE is located at Social Science, where I took the course in French  'Géographie et écologie urbaine’, which was super interesting (about the evolution of cities and future sustainable cities and ways of living, all with a very critical approach). The couses I took from environmental science were very very good as well - my overall favourite course of them all was "BES Assessing the Multiple Values of Nature", about human-nature relationships, NCP's and more modern and inclusive ways of valuing ecosystems and Ecosystem Services. We did some interesting GIS work (recreation map of nature using SoME posts) and talked about environmental ethics having philosphical discussions. The teacher Martin Schlaepfer is incredibly good. 
“FND Climatic Change" was an easy version of "globale geosystemer" and very introductory - can recommend if you’re studying geography at UCPH and want an easy and non-stresseful course (no assignments, only lectures, that I just went quickly through before the exam, still went good).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Look at which courses have an exam at the end and which ones don't!! Because I ended up having 7 courses in total but "only" 3 exams in January, because some of the courses had a presentation in December as the "final exam". Was very nice that I only had 3 exams. Some other students at the uni had a little more than me or none at all.

If you are able to speak a bit of French and want to be better at it (I had done Fransk A in highschool, but not spoken until the summer before my exchange), I recommend taking at least one real uni-course in French. Even though it sounds crazy hard, it’s worth it and not so hard. After 1 or 2 months I got into it and ended up doing an oral exam in partly French (Frenglish). I really did a lot of progress with my French speaking skills. A lot of exchange students choose French courses at uni even though they are not fluent at all, so you're not alone being bad at it in the beginning. I only took one, but almost regret not doing more courses in French. It was hard in the beginning, but then suddenly clicked and got easy - honestly totally doable, and so happy I improved my French to a level where I can read and speak it kinda fluently now.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Before coming to L'UNIGE, I did a 3-week language course at UCPH during the summer holidays (they send you e-mails out about this opportunity a couple months before the courses start), which taught me a lot/got me back into speaking French and I met other nice students, who was going on exchange the same place as me or other French-speaking places for their exchange.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Lower than UCPH, but depends on courses + faculty. Social Science was known for being a bit lower than UCPH, Economy and Management is easier if you choose “management” courses, but the “economy” courses are haaard. Science is in a general pretty high level - but the environmental science department at the Science faculty is the same at UCPH, I’d say, maybe a little bit lower level… or at least I found it easier to get higher grades.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Pretty much the same.. maybe a bit more of lectures and less class teaching and discussions than UCPH….

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: “T206059 - Géographie et écologie urbaine”, “S240009 "The Many Faces of Philanthropy”, E4E187 "Assessing the Multiple Values of Nature”, “T207003 - Emotions, behaviors and collective action”, “14E150 - FND Climatic Change”, “SA24 - Grammaire B1 at MDL, “SA24 - Expression orale” at MDL.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: “BES Assessing the Multiple Values of Nature”!! It also included a city walk in Geneva, where we learned about the nature and biodiversity initiatives. And “Géographie et écologie urbaine”. L’UNIGE is a good university for urban geography (or human geography in general) - mostly their French courses though. Heard good things about “Histoire écologique du monde contemporain” (about cities, (urban) ecology etc.) + the course “Cities in transition” (they had a super interesting field trip/excursion) and “Cities and Social Change”. I was allowed to take some master-courses that were really interesting.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Fees for getting the residence permit (approx 500 DKK) + a fine in the bus of 800 DKK for not having a valid ticket:(

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
You get the SEMP-scholarship as an exchange student from the EU at L’UNIGE. This is similar to the Erasmus scholarship (approx 4000 DKK per month). I didn’t end up spending that much more money than I came with on my exchange - I had the SU, SEMP-scholarship and got a private scholarship from Hedeselskabet of 12000 DKK.  

In general Geneva is known for being cheaper compared to other cities in Switzerland e.g. Zürich. When buying groceries in Lidl + having a La Farce membership (volunteer-driven organisation that gives out free food once a week) I ended up spending almost less money on groceries than i Cph. You can also go to France (10 mins away) and food is cheaper. 
Meat and fish is extremely expensive in all over Switzerland though, but as a vegetarian it’s fine. Free public transportation for students of 25 or younger. Doing trips to other places in Switzerland is expensive - that’s why I got a half-fare travel card (can recommend if going a lot on hikes/visits to other cities in Switzerland). Wine and beer at stores is pretty cheap. 
There are many free sport-activities at the university too.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Easy enrolment of sport activities and welcoming associations at L’UNIGE.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
So so many associations/clubs, and they are super welcoming for new students + Exchange students. The EDD Association for “Students supporting sustainable development” is nice, they hosted an apéro (kind of student bar event) at their beautiful urban rooftop garden at Uni Dufour (view of the alps etc) in the beginning of the semester, that I joined and met people that became my friends. All the associations are good places to meet people and locals. You can also just join their events, like the apéro’s (what I did) and especially in the beginning of the semester. I was too busy to join an association fully, but if staying a year, I’d totally have done it. 
Very good university sport activities too - me and some friends signed up for funk dance class, and had a lot of fun.  They have so many different types of sports classes.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Volunteer at La Farce (volunteer-driven organisation that gives out free food once a week with a chili, alternative vibe), a lot of local + exchange students join it and you can get a subscription for free to collecting food once a week (fresh veggies, eggs, pasta etc.) and it’s a very vibrant and cute social spot with free events like hip hop classes, free guestlist to cool technoclub Le Zoo, free french classes, parties, free restaurant visits every monday and more. I met nice people while having a couple shifts as a volunteer there. I also spoke and improved my French + I saved so much money on groceries.
There are lot of things happening in Geneva and many different types of people (more diversity than I’ve experienced in CPH), you just have to look for them (for example at events, uni and parties).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
- Hang out at Bains des Pâquis: Sun bathing, winter dipping, doing saunas og hammams. Also the very best place to eat cheese fondue in a relaxed atmosphere.
- The city is all about knowing when and where the fun and cool events are happening, otherwise some places can seem a bit empty - events appear on flyers + posters on the streets and on the website
Ladecadanse.ch
- Go to the cute student bar, Datcha for a fun vibe and cheap drinks
- Go to the Halloween party at Village du Soir, where all students in Geneva go in fall
- Go hiking at Mont Salève, Jura Mountains, Charmonix etc. - you can use the Komoot app for finding hike routes
- Best clubs: Le Zoo + L'Atelier (at l'Usine), Motel Campo, La Gravière
- Best bars: L'écurie + Les Grottes area. Also all the way up and down the street Rue de l'École de Médecine is crowded with people
- Go to the MAMCO Contemporary Art Museum for free pre-drinks (free alcohol and snacks) and entrance at beautiful art exhibitions and parties
- Best coffee + pain suisse (Swiss pain au chocolat): Les Petites Artisanes, MAME, Beau Coffee
- Mingle with other international exchange students at ESN events (they have city walks, fondue nights, they are best in the beginning) and locals (via courses, La Farce, going out)
- Places easy worth visiting and easy to reach by train: Lausanne, Zürich (Switzerland), Other countries: Grenoble, Lyon, Turin. I also went to Montpellier which was lovely

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy, very much like Danish culture. Though I do think that local people and students are more open to chat and mingle with exchange students than in DK - but might also be due to the fact that Geneva is such an international city, everyone is from everywhere.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Like mentioned before, classes (just be proactive, ask for their number and go for coffee), language tandem/buddy, La Farce or uni-associations

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The strict dorm rules at La Cité Universitaire, where you have to be quiet after 22:30, otherwise if you’re being too loud talking to people in the kitchen, the guard will come and tell you to go to bed and be quiet…

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That it’s such an international environment in Geneva, mostly all of the students at the University of Geneva come from other places than the city itself - either other parts of Switzerland or other countries. Many people are international and have studied abroad for a longer time. That means no one seems narrow-minded and most are interested in getting to know you and hearing about where you’re from and your culture etc. I also appreciate that you can go to so many different beautiful cities within a short distance of eachother, fx just within Switzerland you can go lovely cities Bern, Lausanne, Basel, Lugano, Zurich and some of the smaller mountain villages. AND you can go to Grenoble, Lyon, Turin, Paris (only 5 hours away by train) and many more cities that are in other countries but close to Geneva/Switzerland - perfect for exploring more of Europe. Good traditional food in Switzerland is a plus too.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Learn French during your exchange at L'UNIGE, it's totally doable. If you know a little it's easier though (but also you can take complete beginner classes (and might get up to 6 ECTS for doing it) too). The main language is French and everything like signs, many e-mails etc. are in French (usually also translated to English). 
2. People studying at L’UNIGE are down-to-earth and level-headed, imo. They are not only there to party. I mostly just went because I wanted to improve my French though:)) 
3. It’s not crazy expensive like you hear people say (since you get both SU + SEMP scholarships, and student accomodation is same price level as in DK) - I heard that Zurich is way more expensive than Geneva 
4. Extra: Do prioritize making sure you don’t miss the welcome week/welcome days the week before the semester starts - this is the social moment to meet people and future friends. Imo it’s best going a week before the welcome week, so you have time to both settle in & going to the welcome week events.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
institution? *
DON’T SPEND TOO MUCH TIME ON UNI, SPEND LESS THAN YOU’RE USED TO AT HOME, YOU’D REGRET IT OTHERWISE. 
There are many exchange-spots for UCPH-students at University of Geneva, which also gives the opportunity to create a Danish-people network - we were around 15 Danish students at University of Geneva and hung out a lot + helped each other with necessary paper work like getting the residence permit and so on. 
The autumn semester goes from Sep-Feb, so people went home for Christmas and exams started in January. I thought this was nice, because then I came back for a more chill study vibe to saying goodbye go Geneva. Also I was lucky to only have 3 exams in the end of January, so didn’t feel that stresset about it. 

Extra adivce: MDL's language courses are also a good place to meet other exchange students. 
- Join the ESN events (Erasmus Student Network) - this is where you meet other exchange students in the beginning of the semester (my good friendgroup was made within the first weeks by meeting people there - specifically the ESN city tour during the welcome week). 
- Volunteer at La Farce
- Join an association (or just their events, like apéro) at L'UNIGE
- Use the apps Totem and The Fork for discounts at cafés, restaurants and stores

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Meeting extremely nice people, that will be my friends for life. 
Becoming fluent in French.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Not having friends and family close by whenever needing them, if feeling down.. but in our friendgroup we became each others family:) And it’s not far away from DK too. 
Exam season was a bit tougher, since it was more exams and a longer study break than I’m used to.. I felt the level in classes was way lower than at geography in UCPH though, (started studying for an exam 24 hours before and got a good grade even though)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: The more you integrate in the Swiss culture, the better the experience, you’ll get, I think. If you get a social network there, learn the language, learning about the culture and where the good and cute spots in the city are, you’ll end up feeling like you’ve got an attachment to the place and feeling more like it’s been a fullfilled exchange. I’ve got friends from Switzerland and all over the world now, that are coming to visit in CPH and I’m gonna visit in the future. But it definitely also took some effort and social energy to mingle with people (and spend a lot of money on coffee dates with friends, but worth it all:)).

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
